newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan worried by U.S. missiles strikes on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Jordan worried by U.S. missiles strikes on Iraq.

text.p: Jordan on Tuesday expressed deep concern over U.S. missile strikes on Iraqi targets and called for restraint to avoid a further escalation of violence.
But Amman, which has campaigned for change in Baghdad since top Iraqi defections last year, steered clear of condemning Tuesday's biggest military strike against Iraq since the 1991 Gulf War.

The United States said the cruise missile attacks were in retaliation for weekend fighting in northern Iraq when Iraqi troops intervened on behalf of a Kurdish faction fighting with another Kurdish group.

"Jordan is following with concern the latest escalation in the situation and the military operations which might return Iraq to the cycle of violence and counter-violence," Information Minister Marwan Muasher told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
"Jordan rejects any attempt to harm Iraq's sovereignty and the unity of its people and territory," he added in a carefully worded statement that dropped any direct reference to its ally, Washington.

Muasher said Jordan had not been used as a base for Tuesday's one-hour assault on southern Iraq, a day after General John Shalikashvili, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, met King Hussein to discuss the situation in northern Iraq.

Prime Minister Abdul Karim al-Kabariti, a fierce critic of Iraq since the king turned against his erstwhile ally Saddam Hussein in August 1995, summoned Iraq's ambassador to Jordan, Nouri el-Wayess, to brief him on Jordan's stand.

Some Jordanian politicians and diplomats said the government appeared to take a more cautious and balanced stand on the operation that has enraged many Jordanians in a kingdom where pro-Iraqi support remains strong.
Amman refused to send troops to join a U.S.-led military operation that liberated Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War. Jordan's move angered Washington and most Western and Gulf Arab allies.
Earlier, Jordan's Islamist-led opposition deputies, in a show of solidarity, met Wayess at the Iraqi embassy to denounce the U.S. cruise missile attack on Baghdad.
